title: Swift Concurrency Part 2: async/await & Task
subtitle: This is Part 2 of a 3-part series on Swift Concurrency, Mainly focused on async/await, Task & asynchronous execution

body.title: How to follow along
body.text: Every code block in this article is a building block. By the end, you'll have a complete working playground you can paste directly into Xcode and run. No network connection needed, we simulate delays with Task.sleep

body.title: From Callbacks to async/await
body.text: If you've been writing iOS apps for a while, you know this pattern:

Two network calls, already unreadable. Three or more and you're in pyramid territory. Error propagation is manual, and forgetting to call [tag]completion[/tag] in one branch is a silent bug.
Here's the same logic with async/await:
Same work. Reads top-to-bottom. Error propagation is automatic via [tag]throws[/tag]. The Swift runtime handles the rest.

body.title: Step 1: The Data Models
body.text: First, a few plain value types that represent the data we'll be "fetching" throughout the article. No networking, no dependencies, just [tag]structs[/tag].

body.title: Step 2: Simulating a Network with Task.sleep
body.text: Real network calls are slow and need a connection. Instead, we'll simulate latency using [tag]Task.sleep(for:)[/tag]. This genuinely suspends the task for the given duration. It's not a busy-wait, so the concurrency behaviour is identical to real network code.
Every function in this article calls [tag]FakeNetwork[/tag]. Swap it for real [tag]URLSession[/tag] calls later and nothing else changes.

body.title: Step 3: async/await: The Basics
body.text: [tag]async[/tag] marks a function as one that can suspend, pause its execution without blocking the underlying thread. [tag]await[/tag] is where a suspension might actually happen.

Key mental model: [tag]await[/tag] does not mean [b]"wait and block."[/b] It means [b]"I might pause here. While I'm paused, the thread is free to run something else. When the result is ready, resume me."[/b]

This is fundamentally different from [tag]Thread.sleep()[/tag] or [tag]DispatchSemaphore.wait()[/tag], which freeze the thread entirely.

body.title: Step 4: Sequential vs Parallel with `async let`
body.text: When two operations are independent, running them sequentially is wasteful:
[tag]async[/tag] let starts both immediately. The [tag]await[/tag] on the tuple collects both results once they're both ready:
The parallel version finishes in [tag]~500ms[/tag], the time of the slower operation instead of [tag]~800ms[/tag]. For real network calls, this difference is significant.

body.title: Step 5: `Task` Bridging into Async
body.text: [tag]async[/tag] / [tag]await[/tag] describes what to do asynchronously. [tag]Task[/tag] is how you start it from a synchronous context, like a SwiftUI [tag].onAppear[/tag], a [tag]viewDidLoad[/tag], or the top level of a playground.

[b]Task Priority[/b]
You can hint at how urgently a task should run:
Priority levels from high to low: [tag].high[/tag], [tag].userInitiated[/tag], [tag].medium[/tag], [tag].low[/tag], [tag].utility[/tag], [tag].background[/tag].

[b]Storing the Handle for Cancellation[/b]
[tag]Task {}[/tag] returns a handle. Store it when you need to cancel in-flight work:

body.title: Step 6: Cancellation - Cooperative, Not Forced
body.text: Cancelling a task sets a flag, it doesn't forcefully stop execution. Your code has to check for the flag and respond. This is called cooperative cancellation.

[tag]Task.sleep[/tag] and Apple's async APIs check cancellation automatically, they throw [tag]CancellationError[/tag] when cancelled without you having to do anything extra. [tag]Task.checkCancellation()[/tag] is for your own loops and long-running work.

body.title: Step 7: `Task.detached` Breaking Away from Context
body.text: A regular [tag]Task {}[/tag] inherits the actor context and priority of where it was created. [tag]Task.detached[/tag] breaks both links:
Use [tag]Task.detached[/tag] when:

list: Work should continue even if the originator is deallocated
You need a deliberately different priority from the caller
The work is completely unrelated to the current UI context

body.text: [b]Don't use[/b] it for most things. Detached tasks lose automatic cancellation propagation from the parent, so you own their entire lifecycle. A plain [tag]Task {}[/tag] is almost always the right choice.

body.title: Step 8: `withTaskGroup: Dynamic` Parallelism
body.text: [tag]async[/tag] let works when you know the number of operations at compile time. For a dynamic collection, an array of IDs use [tag]withTaskGroup:[/tag]
All [tag]addTask[/tag] calls start immediately and run concurrently. If any task throws, the group cancels the rest automatically.

body.title: The Complete Playground
body.text: Everything above in a single file. Paste it into an Xcode Playground and run.

body.code:
=== Sequential vs Parallel ===
  Sequential: 0.80s
  Parallel:   0.50s
=== Task Priority ===
  [userInitiated] fetching user...
  [background] sending notification...
  📬 Notification sent to user 99: "Hello!"
  [userInitiated] done
=== Cancellation ===
  ✓ Processed: "Understanding Actors"
  ✓ Processed: "async/await in Practice"
  ⛔ Processing cancelled mid-way
=== Task.detached ===
  [detached] running independently...
  📬 Notification sent to user 1: "Detached sync done"
=== withTaskGroup (3 profiles in parallel) ===
  User 1: 3 posts
  User 3: 3 posts    ← order may vary, tasks complete as they finish
  User 2: 3 posts
  Finished in 0.51s (vs ~2.40s sequential)
✅ All done

body.text: The two numbers worth paying attention to:

list: Sequential vs Parallel: 0.80s → 0.50s. In a real app with slow network calls, this gap is much larger.
Task group: 3 profiles fetched in 0.51s instead of ~2.40s. Each profile takes ~800ms sequentially; the group runs all three at once.

rows: One async call from a sync context
Long loop that should respect cancellation
Work that must outlive its caller

body.title: Summary
body.text: [tag]await[/tag] suspends, it doesn't block. The thread is freed while you wait for a result.
[tag]async[/tag] let parallelises independent work, use it whenever two operations don't depend on each other.
[tag]Task {}[/tag] bridges sync → async. Store the handle when you need cancellation control.
Cancellation is cooperative. Call [tag]Task.checkCancellation()[/tag] inside your own loops; Apple APIs handle it for you.
[tag]Task.detached[/tag] breaks the parent link, reach for it intentionally, not as a default.
[tag]withTaskGroup[/tag] handles dynamic concurrency, all tasks start at once, results collected as they arrive.
